why: Many developers now use AI coding tools every day: Copilot in the IDE, Cursor, Claude Code in the terminal. Recruiters in Tunisia and in Europe have started asking about them in interviews. But these tools can make you faster... or help you ship bugs and security holes faster. This course teaches you to use them like a professional: context, plan, tests, review, security, and how to learn with them instead of just copying.
outcome: Tell autocomplete, chat and agents apart and pick the right tool, write a good CLAUDE.md, run an agent with a plan and small diffs, use tests to protect your code, review AI-written code, keep your secrets safe, and explain your workflow in an interview.

lessons.title: The landscape: autocomplete, chat and agents
text: When we say 'AI coding tools', we mean 3 families. The first is autocomplete (code completion). You type in the IDE, the tool suggests the next line or a whole function in grey, and you press Tab if you like it. GitHub Copilot made the idea popular, and many editors now have something similar. Autocomplete is fast and does not break your flow, but it sees only a little context: the file you have open and a few nearby files.

The second family is chat in the IDE. You select some code and ask 'what does this do?' or 'write a test for this function', and the answer shows up in a side panel. Copilot Chat, Cursor (an editor built on VS Code with AI at its core) and other extensions work this way. It is great for understanding code, asking about an error or drafting a small piece. But you are the one who copies, runs and decides.

The third family is agents (agentic coding tools). Here you do not ask for a piece of code: you give a mission ('add pagination to the /orders endpoint and test it'). The agent reads the repo, searches the files, edits several of them, runs commands (tests, linter, build), looks at the result and tries again until it is done. Claude Code, Anthropic's tool, belongs to this family: you launch it in the terminal (CLI), in the desktop app, on the web, or through IDE extensions such as VS Code and JetBrains. Cursor and Copilot have added agent modes too. As we saw in the Claude API course, agent = model + tools + loop; here the tools are a developer's tools: read a file, write a file, run a command.

When do you use each one? Autocomplete for code you already know and want to write faster: boilerplate, similar tests, mapping. Chat when you want to understand something or ask about a precise piece. An agent when the mission touches several files and needs commands to run: refactoring, a small feature with tests, a migration, investigating a bug. But an agent is not magic: when the mission is vague or the repo has no tests, it can build something big and wrong with great confidence.

The general rule: the more autonomy a tool gets, the more context and control you need. And do not forget that many things need no AI at all: the IDE's own rename and refactor never get it wrong. For prices and plans, check each tool's official pages: they change often, and your company may already have made a choice (lesson 6).
points: Autocomplete: fast, small context, you finish and decide.
Chat in the IDE: understand and ask; you copy and run.
Agent: reads, edits and runs commands on its own in a loop.
More autonomy = more context, tests and review.

example.code:
Need                                   Best fit
-------------------------------------  ----------------------------------
Finish the line, boilerplate           Autocomplete (Copilot, Cursor...)
"What does this function do?"          Chat in the IDE
Fix a failing test across 4 files      Agent (Claude Code, agent modes)
Explore an unknown repository          Agent or chat, read-only first
Rename a variable in one file          The IDE's own refactor, no AI
example.note: Not everything needs AI: the IDE's refactor is deterministic and does not make mistakes.

lessons.title: Running an agent: context, plan, small steps and review
text: The agent does not know your project the way you do. It does not know why this table has two date columns, or who still uses the old endpoint. If you give it a one-sentence mission, it fills the gaps with assumptions. So the first rule is context. Tell it the goal (not just the task), which files matter, the constraints (do not change the public API, do not add a dependency), and how it will know it is done (which tests must pass).

The second rule: a plan before the code. Ask it to read and propose a plan without changing anything. Claude Code has plan mode for exactly this: the agent only searches and reads, then gives you a plan to read and correct. A wrong plan takes a minute to fix; 400 wrong lines take an hour. And when you read the plan, you often find out that you were not clear about what you wanted either.

The third rule: small steps. Split a big mission ('rewrite the payment module'): tests first, then the refactoring, then the feature. Each step = a small diff you read, tests you run, and a commit. When a step goes wrong, you go back to the previous commit instead of digging through 30 changed files. Git is your seat belt: one branch per mission, and small commits.

The fourth rule: review every diff. The agent may change something you never asked for: delete a test because it fails, add a try/except that swallows the error, or edit a file that has nothing to do with the task. Claude Code shows you the diff and asks for permission before it edits a file or runs a command (depending on your settings). Do not say 'yes' every time without reading: blind 'yes' is how bugs get in.

And when the agent gets confused (it repeats the same mistake, or the conversation gets too long), do not let it go round in circles: stop it, tell it what the mistake is, or start a new session with a clean context and a short summary. The context window is large but not infinite, and a conversation full of failed attempts confuses the model even more.
points: Context: the goal, the files, the constraints and a 'done' criterion.
A plan before the code; plan mode when you can.
Small step = small diff = easy review = commit.
Read every diff; no blind 'yes'.
When it gets confused: stop it, clarify, or start a new session.

example.code:
Goal: customers must be able to page through their orders
(the mobile app loads 2,000 orders at once today).

Task: add pagination to GET /orders in api/orders.py.
- Query params: page (default 1) and page_size (default 20, max 100).
- Keep the response backward compatible: add "page" and "total", do not rename fields.
- Do not add new dependencies.

Done when: the existing tests pass and new tests cover page 1,
the last page and page_size > 100.

First read the relevant files and propose a short plan.
Do not edit anything until I approve the plan.
example.note: The prompt gives the why, the what, the constraints and the criterion, and asks for a plan before any change.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md: the project's instructions
text: Every new session, the agent starts from zero: it does not remember what you told it yesterday. The fix: an instructions file it reads by itself at the start. In Claude Code, that is CLAUDE.md: a markdown file at the root of the repo, which Claude Code adds to the context automatically in every session. You can also put a CLAUDE.md in a subfolder (instructions specific to one part of the code), and a personal one in your user folder for your preferences across all projects. The /init command drafts a first version from the repo, and you correct it.

What goes in it? First, the commands: how to install, run the tests, the linter, the build. This is what helps the most: without it the agent guesses ('npm test? pytest? make?') and wastes time. Second, the conventions: the style, the folder structure, the libraries you use (and the ones you do not), how to name files. Third, the rules: 'do not touch the old migrations', 'every new endpoint needs a test', 'never commit directly to main'.

Keep it short and precise. CLAUDE.md enters the context in every session: every line costs tokens and takes a bit of the model's attention. 'Write clean code' is useless: the model knows that. 'Use httpx, not requests' is useful. And do not fill the file with 'IMPORTANT' on every line: when everything is important, nothing is.

CLAUDE.md is a living file. When you see the agent repeat the same mistake (using the wrong library, forgetting to activate the venv), add a line. Commit it to the repo so the whole team benefits, and review changes to it like code. And never put a secret in it: the file is in Git, read by the whole team and by the model.

Other tools have the same idea under other names: Copilot reads a repository instructions file, Cursor has project rules, and many tools now read AGENTS.md. The name changes, the principle stays: the information the agent cannot guess, written short and precise.
points: CLAUDE.md at the root is read in every session; /init drafts a first version.
Commands, conventions and rules: what the agent cannot guess.
Short and precise: every line takes room in the context.
Commit it, review it, add to it when a mistake repeats, and no secrets in it.

example.code:
# CLAUDE.md

## Project
Django API for a Tunisian delivery startup. Python 3.12, PostgreSQL.

## Commands
- Install: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
- Run tests: pytest -q
- Lint and format: ruff check . && ruff format .
- Run locally: python manage.py runserver

## Conventions
- Business logic goes in services/, not in views.
- Use httpx for HTTP calls, not requests.
- Money is stored in millimes (integer), never as float.
- Every new endpoint needs tests in tests/api/.

## Rules
- Never edit existing files in migrations/; create a new migration.
- Never read or print .env files.
- Run pytest and ruff before saying a task is done.
example.note: The agent cannot guess these on its own: millimes, httpx, the migrations.

lessons.title: Tests: your safety net
text: AI-written code can look right and still be wrong. Reviewing it by eye catches a lot, but not everything: edge cases, rounding, a date in a time zone... Tests are the proof that the code does what you want, and that tomorrow's change did not break anything. With an agent, tests matter even more: the agent can run the tests itself, see what fails and fix it, as long as the tests exist and the command is written in CLAUDE.md.

Ask for tests precisely. Not 'add tests', but: 'write pytest tests for apply_discount: the normal case, an unknown code, an expired code, and rounding to the millime'. Then read the tests before the code: a test that checks nothing ('assert result is not None') protects nothing. A good test checks a precise result.

TDD with AI: the order that works well. (1) You (or the agent) write tests that say what you want. (2) You run them and see them fail: if they do not fail, the test checks nothing or the feature already exists. (3) Commit the tests. (4) Tell the agent: 'implement it so the tests pass, and do not change the tests'. That way the tests become the specification, and the agent has a clear criterion for knowing it is done.

Do not let the agent 'fix' a test by changing the test. This is one of the most common mistakes: a test fails, the agent changes the assertion or adds a skip, and everything turns green. When you read the diff, any change to an existing test needs a clear reason. Also: tests the agent writes for code it wrote itself can repeat the same misunderstanding. So write at least one test for the important case yourself, or check it carefully by eye.

CI (GitHub Actions or another) completes the picture: every pull request runs the tests, and you never merge AI code that has not passed them. And in AI applications (prompts, models), tests are called evals: that is the topic of the evaluation course (ai-evals).
points: Tests are the proof, not your impression when you read the code.
Ask for precise cases, and read the tests before the code.
TDD: failing tests, commit, then implementation without changing the tests.
A changed or skipped test in a diff = alert.

example.note: After the commit, the prompt: 'Implement apply_discount so these tests pass. Do not modify the tests.'

lessons.title: Reviewing AI code: what to look for
text: AI code comes out clean, tidy, with comments... and that is exactly what makes you trust it more than you should. Review AI code as seriously as a colleague's code (or more). There are 4 things to always look for.

First, security. A SQL query built with an f-string (SQL injection), user input that is not validated, a file opened from a path the user supplies, a secret written in the code, CORS open to everyone, verify=False on an HTTPS request 'to make it work'. The model learned from public code, and public code is full of these mistakes. Every endpoint, every query, everything that touches auth: read it yourself.

Second, APIs that do not exist (hallucinated APIs). The model can use a function that does not exist in the library, a parameter from another version, or a package whose name is close to a real one. That last case is dangerous: if a package with that name exists on PyPI or npm and someone published it with bad intentions, you install it with your own hands. Before adding a dependency, check that the package exists, is well known, and is the one you want. Tests and the linter catch many wrong functions; packages need your eyes.

Third, licences. A long piece of code can be very close to existing code under a licence (GPL, for example). Some tools have a filter for this, and companies have policies. A practical rule: do not accept a long piece of code you do not understand and whose origin you do not know, and when you add a library, check its licence against your company's policy.

Fourth, over-engineering. You asked for a function and got a module with 3 classes, an interface, a factory and a config. Or the agent added error handling, retries and logs everywhere. More code = more bugs and less review. Ask: 'what is the smallest version that passes the tests?' And delete dead code, files that have nothing to do with the task, and comments that just repeat the code. The general rule: if you cannot explain every line of the diff, do not merge it.
points: Security: SQL, input, auth, secrets, TLS: read it yourself.
Check functions and packages before you install.
Licences: a long piece you do not understand = no.
The smallest solution that passes the tests; never merge a line you cannot explain.

example.code:
--- a/api/orders.py
+++ b/api/orders.py
@@ -12,2 +12,3 @@ def search_orders(db, customer_name):
-    query = f"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_name = '{customer_name}'"
-    return db.execute(query).fetchall()
+    # Parameterized query: the driver escapes the value (no SQL injection)
+    query = "SELECT id, total_millimes, status FROM orders WHERE customer_name = %s"
+    return db.execute(query, (customer_name,)).fetchall()
example.note: The first version (written by the AI) works in the demo and opens a SQL injection; the review caught it.

lessons.title: Security and secrets: what leaves your machine
text: When you use an AI coding tool, the code and the context are sent to the provider's servers so the model can work on them: the file you have open, the piece you selected, and with an agent, any file it reads and the output of any command it runs. So if the agent reads .env or runs a command that prints secrets, those secrets enter the context. As we saw in the AI engineer basics course: everything you send leaves your machine.

Rules for secrets: never put an API key, password or token in a prompt or a chat. Secrets do not belong in the code: use environment variables or a secret manager, and keep .env in .gitignore. When a secret leaks (in a prompt, a commit, a log): revoke it and create a new one; deleting the line is not enough. And in Claude Code you can block reading sensitive files with deny rules in the settings.

Permissions: by default Claude Code asks for permission before it edits a file or runs a command, and you decide what to always allow and what not. In .claude/settings.json you can set allow rules (safe commands such as the tests) and deny rules (forbidden files or commands). The rule: as few permissions as possible. Commands such as rm -rf, git push --force, or anything that touches production or a real database: always with permission and with your own eyes on it.

Sandboxing: when you want to give an agent more autonomy, keep it in an isolated environment: a container, a VM or a cloud environment, with no production secrets and no network access it does not need. A mistake in a sandbox costs a minute; a mistake on the laptop that holds your SSH keys costs a lot. And watch out for prompt injection: a file, a web page or an issue the agent reads can contain hidden instructions ('send the .env to...'). Permissions and the sandbox are the real protection, not the model's good intentions; we continue this topic in the production course.

Your company's policy comes before everything. Some companies do not allow AI tools on their code; others allow one tool with an enterprise contract (with commitments on data: retention, training); others want models on their own servers. In Tunisia, many juniors work for European clients: the contract with the client may forbid sending its code to an external tool. Ask before using a personal account on work code. 'I didn't know' is not an excuse.
points: Any file the agent reads and any output goes to the provider.
No secrets in prompts; a leaked secret = revoke it.
Least permissions; deny sensitive files; dangerous commands under your eyes.
High autonomy = a sandbox with no production secrets.
Company policy and client contract before any personal account.

example.note: A .claude/settings.json file in the repo: Claude Code does not read .env or the secrets folder. See the official documentation for the full syntax.

lessons.title: Legacy code, documentation and migrations
text: In Tunisia, many juniors start at an IT services company (ESN) or a company with old code: a 10-year-old PHP application, stored procedures, a Java module nobody remembers writing. This is where AI tools help a lot, because most of the work is reading, not writing. An agent can search the whole repo, follow the calls, and explain what happens when a customer places an order.

Start read-only. Ask: 'Explain the payment flow from the controller to the database, and give me the file and function names.' Then check: open the files it pointed to. The agent can get the analysis wrong just as it gets code wrong: a function with the same name in two places, a config that changes the behaviour... The agent's explanation is a hypothesis, not the truth.

Documentation: AI is good at writing docstrings, READMEs, architecture diagrams (as text or Mermaid) and onboarding notes. But wrong docs are worse than no docs. Check everything, especially the 'why' (why the code is written this way): the model cannot know it unless it is written down somewhere. Ask the team and add the why yourself.

Migrations (Python 2 to 3, AngularJS to Angular, Java 8 to 17, a framework upgrade): the approach that works: (1) tests on the current behaviour before any change (characterization tests: they check what the code does today, even if it has a bug); (2) a plan in small steps; (3) migrate module by module, each step with green tests and a commit; (4) review carefully when the agent uses a new API: that is where hallucinations hide, because the model can mix up versions.

It looks long, but it goes well with an agent: the agent can write the characterization tests, and you check that they reflect the real behaviour. And at every step, the diff stays small and readable. That way the migration that was 'a 6-month project nobody wants to touch' becomes small steps you can deliver within the sprint.
points: Legacy: AI helps most with reading and understanding.
Start read-only; the agent's explanation is a hypothesis to check.
Wrong docs are worse than no docs; a human provides the 'why'.
Migration: characterization tests, plan, module by module, a commit per step.

example.code:
Read-only task: do not edit any file.

Explain how an order is paid in this repository:
1. Entry point (route or controller) and the main functions called, in order.
2. Where the payment status is written to the database.
3. Anything surprising: duplicated logic, dead code, hard-coded values.

For each point, give the file path and function name so I can check it myself.
If you are not sure about something, say so instead of guessing.
example.note: A file and function name with every claim: you can check it yourself.

lessons.title: Your career: learn with AI, don't just copy
text: The big risk for a junior is not that AI takes their job: it is ending up unable to work without AI, and not understanding the code they merge. In an interview, when debugging a production outage, or when the tool gets it wrong, your understanding is what makes the difference. A recruiter can ask you about any line of a project in your portfolio: if you cannot explain it, the project works against you.

How to learn with it: ask 'why', not just 'how'. When the agent fixes a bug, ask it to explain the cause. Try first yourself (15-20 minutes), then compare with the AI's solution. Ask it to review your code instead of writing it. Sometimes write code on your own (katas, exercises) without AI, like an athlete who trains without machines. And when it uses something you do not know (a decorator, a generator, a SQL index), read the official documentation.

Keep a small log: every week, 3 things you learned from your AI sessions (a bug, a pattern, a command). It helps you understand and it helps in interviews too. And in your projects or in open source, commits and PR descriptions should be written with understanding: what you changed and why, not a generic summary written by the AI.

In interviews: be honest. Many companies now ask 'do you use AI tools? how?'. The good answer is neither 'no, never' nor 'the AI writes everything'. The good answer: a clear workflow (context and CLAUDE.md, plan, small steps, tests, review, security) and a real example: 'the agent suggested a package that does not exist, and I caught it in review'. Some companies run live exercises without AI, others with AI: prepare for both.

On the market, remote work with European companies and freelancing ask for productivity, but also quality and trust. A developer who knows how to work with an agent safely (tests, review, secrets) is much stronger than one who works without AI, and than one who uses AI blindly. That is the skill to put on your CV: 'AI-assisted development with tests and code review', not just a tool name.
points: Understanding makes the difference: never merge a line you cannot explain.
Try first, compare after; ask for reviews and explanations.
A small log: 3 things learned every week.
In interviews: a clear workflow + a real example.

example.code:
Learning log - week 12

1. Bug: duplicate orders on double click.
   The agent's first fix added a sleep(); I rejected it.
   Real cause: no unique constraint. Fix: unique (customer_id, cart_id) + a test.
2. Learned: pytest fixtures with yield (setup + teardown).
3. Caught in review: the agent imported a package that does not exist on PyPI.

Interview version (30 seconds):
"I use an agent for multi-file changes, but I plan first, keep diffs small,
run the tests and review every line before I merge."
example.note: This log helps you learn and gives you real examples for interviews.

exercises.q: Which tool (autocomplete, chat in the IDE, agent, or no AI) would you use, and why: (a) writing 15 similar DTO mapping fields, (b) a bug that fails a test in a module you do not know, (c) renaming a variable in one file, (d) upgrading a library across 20 files with tests?
exercises.hint: Think about the number of files, the commands that need to run, and the risk.
exercises.answer: (a) Autocomplete: repetitive code you know, you finish with Tab and read it. (b) Chat or an agent, read-only first: it explains the module and the cause, then you fix it with a small diff and a test. (c) No AI: the IDE's rename is deterministic. (d) Agent: many files and the tests must run; a plan first, module by module, a commit per step and a review of every diff.

exercises.q: This agent prompt is not good: 'add login to the app'. Rewrite it with context, constraints and a 'done' criterion.
exercises.hint: The goal, the files, no new dependency, which tests, and a plan before any change.
exercises.answer:
Goal: users of our Flask app must log in with e-mail and password
before they can see /dashboard.

Context: users are in the users table (models/user.py); passwords are not stored yet.
Constraints:
- Hash passwords with werkzeug.security (already installed); no new dependencies.
- Do not change existing routes other than /dashboard.
- Never log passwords.

Done when: pytest passes, with new tests for a correct login, a wrong password
and /dashboard without login (redirect to /login).

First read the code and propose a plan. Do not edit files until I approve it.

exercises.q: Write a short CLAUDE.md for a FastAPI project: Python 3.12, pytest tests in tests/, linting with ruff, migrations with Alembic (do not touch the old migrations), dates always in UTC, and the agent must not read .env.
exercises.hint: 3 sections: Commands, Conventions, Rules. Short and precise.
exercises.answer:
# CLAUDE.md

## Commands
- Run tests: pytest -q
- Lint and format: ruff check . && ruff format .
- New migration: alembic revision --autogenerate -m "<message>"

## Conventions
- Python 3.12, FastAPI.
- Store and compare dates in UTC; convert only for display.
- Tests live in tests/, one file per router.

## Rules
- Never edit existing files in alembic/versions/; always create a new migration.
- Never read or print .env files.
- Run pytest and ruff before saying a task is done.

exercises.q: To do TDD with an agent, write the tests before the code for a function normalize_phone(text) that returns a Tunisian number in the format +216XXXXXXXX: '22 123 456', '+216 98 765 432', '00216 55 000 111', and a number that is too short must raise ValueError.
exercises.hint: One test per case, and pytest.raises for the invalid case.

exercises.q: The agent gave you code with: requests.get(url, verify=False), an import of 'fastjsonx' (a library you have never heard of), and a ConfigFactory class for a function that reads a single variable. What do you say in the review?
exercises.answer: 1) verify=False turns off TLS certificate verification: someone could read or modify the traffic. Remove it; if the certificate is internal, use its CA. 2) fastjsonx: check that the package exists, is well known and is the one you want; it is often a guessed name or one close to a real package, and someone may have published a malicious package under that name. If Python's json is enough, use it. 3) ConfigFactory: over-engineering; os.environ.get in a single function is enough. Ask for the smallest version that passes the tests.

exercises.q: An old test fails after a change the agent made. In the diff you see that the agent changed the assertion from == 45_000 to == 44_999. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Do not accept the change. The test was passing before: that means the new code changed the behaviour, not that the test is wrong. Restore the test as it was, and tell the agent: 'This test was passing before your change. Fix the code, do not modify the test, and explain what changed the result.' If, after analysis, the test really is wrong (a business rule changed), you change it yourself with the reason written in the commit, after checking with the team.

exercises.q: By mistake, you pasted a production API key into a chat with an AI coding tool so it could 'explain an error'. What are the steps?
exercises.answer: 1) Revoke the key right away in the provider's console and create a new one; deleting it from the chat is not enough, because the key has already left your machine. 2) Replace the key wherever you use it (secret manager, environment variables). 3) Check the usage logs for any strange usage. 4) Tell your manager or the security team, as the policy requires. 5) Afterwards, add a deny rule for .env and use placeholders such as <API_KEY> when you paste an error into the chat.

pitfalls: Accepting every diff with 'yes' without reading it: the agent can delete a test, swallow an error or edit a file that has nothing to do with the task.
Giving a big, vague mission in one sentence: the agent fills the gaps with assumptions and builds something big and wrong. Context, a plan, and small steps.
Letting the agent 'fix' a test by changing the assertion or adding a skip: CI turns green and the bug stays.
Installing a package the AI suggested without checking that it exists and is well known: it may be made up or malicious.
Putting an API key, a password or client data in a prompt, or letting the agent read .env: everything in the context goes to the provider.
Using a personal AI account on company or client code without asking about the policy and the contract.
Merging code you cannot explain: in an interview or during an incident, it will expose you.

interview.q: How do you use AI coding tools in your work?
interview.a: Autocomplete for repetitive code, chat to understand code or an error, and an agent such as Claude Code for changes that touch several files. With the agent: clear context and a CLAUDE.md, a plan before the code, small steps with commits, tests, and a review of every diff before the merge. And I have a real example: in a review, I caught a package the agent suggested that does not exist.

interview.q: What is the difference between autocomplete, chat and an agent?
interview.a: Autocomplete suggests the next line from a small context and you finish it. Chat answers a question about selected code, and you copy and run the result. An agent takes a mission, reads the repo, edits several files and runs commands in a loop until it is done. The more autonomy grows, the more context, tests and review you need.

interview.q: What do you put in a CLAUDE.md or a project instructions file?
interview.a: What the agent cannot guess: the commands (install, tests, lint, build), the conventions (structure, libraries, naming) and the rules (do not touch the old migrations, a test for every endpoint). Short and precise, because it is read in every session and takes room in the context. Committed to the repo, reviewed like code, and no secrets in it.

interview.q: How do you know AI-written code is correct?
interview.a: Not from an impression. Tests before the code (TDD), or at least tests for the important cases, CI running them on every PR, and a review with my own eyes: security, APIs and packages that actually exist, licences, and over-engineering. And I watch for the agent changing or skipping a test: that is an alert.

interview.q: What are the security risks of using an agent on the repo?
interview.a: The code, any file it reads and any output go to the provider, so secrets can enter the context. The agent can run dangerous commands, and it can read content that contains prompt injection. The protection: secrets in environment variables, deny on .env, least permissions, dangerous commands under my own eyes, a sandbox for high autonomy, and the company's policy.

interview.q: How do you use AI on legacy code or a migration?
interview.a: I start read-only: I ask for an explanation of the flow with file and function names, and I check it myself. Then characterization tests on the current behaviour, a plan in steps, a migration module by module with a commit and tests at each step, and a careful review of the new APIs, because the model can mix up versions.

interview.q: Don't AI tools reduce the need for juniors? How do you learn with them?
interview.a: They change what is expected from a junior: more review, tests and understanding, less writing by hand. I use them to learn: I try first and compare, I ask for explanations and reviews, I read the documentation when something new comes up, and I keep a log of what I learned. And I never merge a line I cannot explain.
